title: Psalm 99: The Holy King Enthroned on the Cherubim
summary: The LORD reigns from Zion, enthroned above the cherubim, and the nations are called to tremble and praise his great and awesome name. He is a King who loves justice and has done justice in Israel. The psalm remembers Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, who called on him and were answered, and it describes him as a God who forgave his people and still dealt with their wrongdoing. Three times it declares that he is holy.
story: Psalm 99 is the last of the kingship psalms that began with Psalm 93 and resumed in Psalms 95 to 98. Where Psalms 96 and 98 widened the view to the nations and all creation, Psalm 99 narrows it back to Zion, to the ark, and to Israel's own history with God. It recalls Israel's great intercessors, Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, figures from the time before and at the start of the monarchy. Book IV keeps reaching back behind David to that older era, and here the point is that God's reign over Israel was a relationship of speaking and answering, forgiveness and discipline, long before there was a human king.
historical:
The psalm has no heading in Hebrew and names no occasion. Its references to the cherubim, the footstool, and the holy mountain assume the temple in Jerusalem, where the ark of the covenant stood in the inner room, the Most Holy Place, beneath two carved cherubim (1 Kings 6:23-28). That has led some scholars to date the psalm before the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC, since the ark disappears from history after that. Others note that later worshipers kept using this language of God's throne even after the ark was gone, and they place the psalm with the other kingship psalms in the period after the exile.

The reference to Samuel is notable. He was not from the priestly family of Aaron, but he offered sacrifices and interceded for Israel (1 Samuel 7:5-9; 12:19-23), and Jeremiah names Moses and Samuel together as the greatest intercessors Israel ever had (Jeremiah 15:1). The psalm uses the word priests loosely, for those who stood between God and the people.
cultural:
Cherubim in the ancient Near East were composite winged creatures, often part lion, part eagle, part human, that guarded thrones and sacred places. Kings in Canaan and Phoenicia were carved sitting on thrones flanked by winged creatures. The ark in Israel's sanctuary had two gold cherubim on its lid, and the space above them was understood as God's invisible throne, with the ark itself as his footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2). Israel made no image of the one seated there. The throne was empty to the eye, which was a startling thing in a world full of divine statues.

Kings were expected to love justice and uphold it, and royal inscriptions boasted of doing so. The psalm says the LORD actually has: “You have exercised justice and righteousness in Jacob” (verse 4). The pillar of cloud recalls the wilderness, where God guided Israel and spoke with Moses at the entrance to the tent of meeting (Exodus 33:9-11).
literary: The psalm is built on a refrain. Each of its three sections ends with a declaration of God's holiness: “He is holy” in verses 3 and 5, and a fuller form in verse 9, “for the LORD our God is holy”. Verses 5 and 9 also share an almost identical call, “Exalt the LORD our God” and worship at his footstool or holy mountain. The threefold holiness has reminded many readers of the seraphim's song in Isaiah 6:3. The sections move from God's rule over the nations (verses 1 to 3), to his justice in Israel (verses 4 and 5), to his dealings with Israel's intercessors (verses 6 to 9). Verse 8 holds two things in careful balance: God forgave, and he also punished.

outline.t: The LORD reigns from Zion over the peoples: He is holy
The King who loves justice: He is holy
Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called, and he answered: the LORD is holy

doctrines.note: Holiness is the psalm's refrain. God is set apart, awesome, and pure, and that holiness is shown in his justice and in the way he deals with sin, not only in the fear he inspires.
Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called on the LORD, and he answered them. The holy King is not unapproachable; he listens to those who stand before him on behalf of others.

Verse 8 holds forgiveness and consequence together: God was “a forgiving God” and also “an avenger of their misdeeds”. The psalm does not explain how both are true, but it refuses to let either cancel the other.

words.note: Qadosh, holy. The root idea is being set apart, belonging to a different order. In the Old Testament it describes God first and things or people only as they belong to him. Its threefold repetition here marks holiness as the heart of God's kingship.

Keruv, cherub. Not a chubby infant, as later art imagined, but a powerful guardian creature. The phrase “enthroned above the cherubim” is an old title of the LORD tied to the ark (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2).

Hadom, footstool. A king's footstool was part of his throne. Here it most likely means the ark (as in 1 Chronicles 28:2), though elsewhere the whole earth is God's footstool (Isaiah 66:1). Worshiping at the footstool is bowing before the King's feet.

Nasa, to lift or carry, here in the sense of forgiving: literally God was a lifting God, one who bore away the people's guilt. The same verb describes carrying burdens, and Exodus 34:7 uses it in God's own description of himself as forgiving iniquity.

christ: The psalm's tension between a God who forgives and a God who does not ignore wrongdoing is one the whole Old Testament carries, and the New Testament says it is resolved at the cross, where God is shown to be both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26). The psalm also honors intercessors who stood between God and a sinful people. The letter to the Hebrews presents Jesus as a priest greater than Aaron who always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25). And the vision of God's throne in Revelation 4, with living creatures crying holy, holy, holy, draws on the same imagery of the holy King enthroned. These are thematic connections, a pattern the psalm sets up and the gospel fills out.

hard.q: How can God be both forgiving and an avenger of his people's misdeeds?
hard.a: Verse 8 seems to say two opposite things about the same people. The wilderness stories explain what it means: Israel's sin with the golden calf was forgiven after Moses' prayer, yet it still brought a plague (Exodus 32:30-35), and Moses and Aaron themselves remained God's servants but were not allowed to enter the land (Numbers 20:12). Forgiveness restored the relationship; it did not erase every consequence. Some interpreters read the “avenger” line as God punishing the people's enemies instead, taking “their misdeeds” as wrongs done to Israel; the Hebrew allows it, though most translations follow the first reading. Either way, the psalm keeps God's mercy from becoming indifference.

questions: The psalm names three people who called on God and were answered. Who has prayed for you in a way that shaped your life?
What is the difference between forgiveness and the removal of every consequence? Where have you seen both in your own story?
Why might an empty throne, with no image of God on it, be a more honest picture of God than any statue?
